title: Check Strings Equal
directAnswer: If lengths differ, return false. Else compare each index; the first mismatch returns false. In Java use `.equals`, never `==` (which compares references).

remember.takeaway: In Java, == on strings is a reference bug — use .equals.
remember.formula: len equal AND every a[i]==b[i]   (Java: use .equals)
antiSignals: Java == on strings — a reference-comparison bug

problemStatement: Given two strings `a` and `b`, return whether they are exactly equal (same length, same characters in order).
understanding: Different lengths → not equal. Otherwise compare character by character.

approaches.name: Character comparison
approaches.whenToMention: This is the standard, expected solution — lead with it.
approaches.explanation:
Two strings are equal when they have the **same length and the same characters in order**. Check length first, then compare character by character, returning false on the first mismatch.

**The Java `==` trap.** In Java, `==` on `String` objects compares *references* (are they the same object?), not contents — so `a == b` can be false for two equal strings. Always use `.equals()` for content equality. This is one of the most common fresher bugs.

**Why length-check first.** Different lengths can't be equal, and the check lets the loop index both strings safely with one bound.

**Python.** `a == b` *does* compare contents, so the language difference itself is worth calling out.

code.python:
def equal(a: str, b: str) -> bool:
    return a == b
